(2) As far as GEA assumes each population occupies only a single environment, which is not true for highly migratory rafting species. According to the population genomic analysis, we found clear geographical population structure within the species, which points to potential local adaptation to the differential environments. We also found many large-scale dispersal organisms showing local adaptation to their breeding ranges, like migratory bird (Bay et al., 2018, Science; Obiol et al., 2025), migratory Arctic fish (Layton et al., 2021).
We have added Discussion as “Despite the importance of rafting processes in marine ecosystems, few previous studies have combined rafting and genomic forecasting in the evaluation of future dispersal potential48. Genetic offset analyses can provide a powerful means to explore the alignment between locally adapted genotypes and the genetic requirements of future marine environments, as highlighted by recent analysis of marine invertebrates49, migratory birds50,51, and fishes52 to evaluate the climate maladaptation. While such offset analyses are yet to fully account for organismal plasticity, the substantial population genomic structure detected here in T. martensii highlights the importance of local adaptation in this rafting species.”
Limitations of Genomic offsets analysis: Genomic offset modeling assumes no plasticity, so the fact that significant plasticity was found under experimental conditions undermines the genomic offset results and should be discussed. Furthermore, much like GEA, genomic offset assumes that populations occupy and are locally adapted to a single environment. Again, as a rafting species, T. martensii experience large environmental fluctuations and local adaptation may be limited in this species. Finally, while forward and reverse genetic offset methods are appropriate for species that can disperse, how dispersal and genomic offset modeling are integrated using ∆D is unclear from the methods. In general, genomic offset predictions have only been empirically tested in a few systems (mostly trees), and these tests have yielded results spanning from inaccurate predictions to relatively accurate predictions. Some empirical validation is needed before using genomic offsets in this system to predict maladaptation.
Response: (1) While gene-expression plasticity is clearly important for rafting individuals experiencing rapid salinity fluctuations, our genomic analysis also reveals strong outlier loci associated with regional salinity variation, revealing an unequivocal signature of local adaptation. In this context, genetic offsets quantify the alignment between this locally adapted genetic composition and the genetic requirements of future environments, which represents the genetic variations required for long-term adaptation of future climate change.
While genomic offset analyses inherently focus on long-term genetic adaptation and do not explicitly incorporate plasticity, our study proposed plasticity as a complementary mechanism acting on distinct temporal scales (short-term dispersal vs. long-term settlement). This integration strengthens our understanding of their adaptive strategies crucial across different spatial and temporal scales. Rather than undermining the validity of genomic offset analyses (which have been undertaken for many marine species), we feel the consideration of both plasticity and genomic offset is valuable for forecasting responses to future environmental scenarios.
(2) As far as the dispersal and genomic offset modelling, we used forward genetic offset to estimate the target location of one species disperse to. Then, we calculated the ∆D between the source and target location to estimate their dispersal possibility, and test whether ocean currents support T. martensii rafting to track suitable habitats. The direction deviation (ΔD) was defined as the angle between the direction of ocean currents and the least-cost path line. The ΔD was calculated as the average of each grid cell along the least-cost path line, and the larger value represents the mismatch between directions of ocean currents and potential dispersal direction. The dispersal velocity (V ) was the average value of ds grid’s effective dispersal velocity, which was calculated as the projection of the ocean current velocity (V ) onto the direction of the path. The transit time between sites was estimated by dividing the least-cost distance by dispersal velocity (Fig. 2a).
We have changed the sentence in the Materials and methods section as “As the GF algorithm and forward genetic offset methods can estimate the target location of species dispersal, we integrated the quantified ocean dynamics with forward offset prediction to test whether the ocean currents can support such dispersal.”
(3) While it is conceivable that such genomic offset analyses could prove inaccurate, our study predicts northward dispersal to track suitable habitats. We note that a variety of marine species, from phytoplankton to fish and marine mammals, have shown direct evidence of such poleward dispersal under climate warming (Hastings et al., 2020). Indeed, several recent studies have combined genetic offset and genomic forecasting in the evaluation of future marine dispersal potential in the marine organisms, for example, ascidians invasion risks along Chinese coasts under climate change (Chen et al., 2024).
We added some Discussion in the revised manuscripts: “Under global change, rafting is likely to present a key mechanism for many marine species tracking their shifting habitats. Along these lines, northward dispersal of T. martensii could potentially mitigate the projected genomic maladaptation of this species under future oceanographic scenarios (Fig. 3b, Supplementary Fig. 13e-g). A wide range of marine species, from phytoplankton to fish and marine mammals, have shown direct evidence of such poleward dispersal under climate warming56.”
We also added some Discussion “Broadly, while our integrative analyses suggest that T. martensii has potential to disperse and adapt to the thermal and osmoregulatory challenges provided by global change (Fig. 6b), shifting oceanographic connectivity patterns may limit its ability to do so. Given the vast numbers of rafting marine species likely to be impacted by forecast marine climate change, there is also an urgent need for further data to help assess and forecast such biological responses. We particularly emphasize the need for additional common garden experiments and temporal genomic studies to further inform marine biodiversity change forecasts and potential management actions.”
Interpretability of gene flow and dispersal modeling: The dispersal and current modeling analyses are unclear, specifically what ∆D actually means - while the authors explain that this is a dispersal direction deviation, it is unclear why dispersal direction would be different from current direction if this species truly lacks autonomous dispersal and instead disperses passively. Figure 2 shows the quantified model and particle trajectory simulations, but does not clarify how ∆D is calculated - is it averaged across all modeled cells, or specific to just the final cell? Furthermore, when doing the gene flow model testing, the authors use K=3 despite recovering K=5 in previous analyses.
Response: (1) The dispersal and currents modeling methods were inspired by the Hodel et al., 2018. It used the Euclidean distance of shortest path between two sites, which should be straight line theoretically. However, islands and lands exist between two sites, and the coastal species couldn’t disperse on the land, therefore, we used the least-cost path on the ocean to represent the dispersal way. The ocean currents variables on the shortest path could be measured its importance in explaining geographic patterns of genetic variation (Hodel et al., 2018). From the source site to the sink site, we identified every grid cell that intersected the least-cost path line. If the ocean currents bearing of a pixel were identical to the bearing of the line, the pixel would be given a score of zero. If the bearing of the pixel were different from the bearing of the line, it would be given a score between zero and 180°, where 180° implies that the ocean current bearing of the pixel is opposite to the line connecting the populations. The ΔD was calculated as the average of each grid cell along the least-cost path line, and the larger value represents the mismatch between directions of ocean currents and potential dispersal direction. Under such a designation, a ∆D value larger than 90° precludes dispersal along the least-cost path.
We have added more definition about the ∆D as: “To test relationships between gene flow and ocean currents, we developed a novel model to quantify ocean currents between two sites based on least-cost dispersal path (Fig. 2a). The direction and velocity of ocean currents play important roles in explaining gene flow between populations26. We defined direction deviation (ΔD) as the angle between the direction of ocean currents and the least-cost path line. The ΔD was calculated as the average of each grid cell along the least-cost path line, and the larger value represents the mismatch between directions of ocean currents and potential dispersal direction. The dispersal velocity (V ) was the average value of ds grid’s effective dispersal velocity, which was calculated as the projection of the ocean current velocity (V ) onto the direction of the path. The transit time between sites was estimated by dividing the least-cost distance by dispersal velocity (Fig. 2a).”
(2) As far as gene flow model testing, we defined groups based on population structure (K=3) to simplify the model prior in the fastsimcoal analysis. Three groups are easy to design genetic models to test the directional or random gene flow. In the revised manuscript, we also tried to use five group (K=5) to perform the simulations, We listed 25 models and also found the northward model is the most likely dispersal models.
We have added all these methods in the Materials and methods section as “We first used five populations (K=5) to infer the potential dispersal hypothesis, and listed 25 models for simulation. The model fitness was evaluated by simulating SFS for each demographic model and comparing the simulated and observed likelihoods. The best demographic model was determined based on the maximum likelihood value. During this process, we found the dispersal hypothesis and model prior could be very complex.”
We also added results in the Results section and supplementary files. “To further infer detailed population migration and gene flow patterns, we performed genetic simulations twice using Fastsimcoal 2.725 with 25 simulation models in five populations (K=5), or 20 simulation models in three populations (K=3) (Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6, Supplementary Table 5). Both simulations suggest asymmetric gene flow, with a northward dispersal model favoured over random and southward dispersal models (Fig. 1g–i).”

Limitations of Plasticity analysis: The salinity stress experiments use a terrestrial species from a different genus than T. martensii, which is the focal species of the rest of the manuscript. While the plasticity analyses themselves seem sound, this calls into question the applicability of these results to marine rafting species, particularly T. martensii. At a minimum the discussion should address how applicable the salinity stress experiments are to the focal species of the manuscript. Additionally, there is significant evidence that plasticity can promote acclimation, but theoretical work suggests that it can also be harmful in the long term by precluding the need for species to genetically adapt to stress (see Ghalambor et. al. 2007). The authors should caveat these results in relevant sections of the discussion.
Response: In the revised manuscript, we collected Talorchestia cf. martensii for salinity experiments and sequenced their transcriptomes, and used the same salinity and duration designation. Moreover, we used longer time treatments to further test for salinity plasticity relevant to long-lived natural rafting voyages. 
(1) In the coastal Talorchestia cf. martensii, we identified numerous differentially expressed genes and pathways among different salinity treatments, which are related to osmoregulation and are differentially expressed only in the gills, not in the legs (Supplementary Table 18), e.g., amino acid transmembrane transport (five genes, GO:0003333), potassium ion transport (four genes, GO:0006813), cell volume homeostasis (three genes, GO:0006884), chloride transport (three genes, GO:0006821). By comparing top10 GO pathways, we found the gills of Talorchestia martensii and Morinoia aosen show a similar function in our analysis.

(5) As far as plasticity can promote acclimation or harmful in the long term, we added some discussion about plasticity in the Discussion section as: “We found increasing differential expression of genes in response to decreasing salinity, with evidence that gills function as the major osmoregulatory organs in maintaining homeostasis under fluctuating salinity58,59. Rapid gene expression shifts suggest plasticity may be a key prerequisite for successful rafting, at least in the short term60 (Fig. 6c). Nevertheless, theoretical studies suggest that, in the longer term, plasticity may slow or constrain populations’ adaptive genetic response to environmental stress61. Therefore, we propose that both short-term (plastic) responses to temporal environmental variation, and longer-lasting adaptive responses to local conditions, should be integrated to understand how rafting species may disperse and respond to future climates.”
Missing details and code: Because the manuscript covers so many topics and fields, detail is sometimes lacking in the main text as to what some of the terms and results actually mean. For example, the distinction between forward and reverse genetic offset is unclear in the main text, and this section would benefit from definitions of these terms that are biologically relevant. This was just one example, but other result and discussion sections would also benefit from additional detail. While the text is already long, clarifying terminology and what each analysis can actually do is important given that it is unlikely that any one reader will be an expert in every field covered in the manuscript.
Response: In our revised manuscripts, we have added the purpose of each analysis, explained more terminology with biologically relevant languages, and streamlined the Discussion section.
For example, about genetic offsets, we added explanation as “To test how rafting crustaceans will respond to future oceanographic change (in the absence of plasticity), we calculated local, forward and reverse genetic offsets29. Specifically, local offset represents the mismatch between current and predicted future genomic variation in the absence of migration. By contrast, forward genetic offset represents the minimum genetic change a population would experience if migrating to a relatively favorable future location, with high values indicating strong mismatches between contemporary and future genetic compositions. Thirdly, reverse genetic offset seeks to assess whether the genotypes required to adapt to future environments already exist within contemporary populations. To this end, we extracted a total of 117,113 SNPs with minor allele frequency > 10%, to predict genetic offset using the gradientForest (GF) approach, a regression tree-based machine-learning algorithm30.”
As far as ΔD, we have explained as “To test relationships between gene flow and ocean currents, we developed a novel model to quantify ocean currents between two sites based on least-cost dispersal path (Fig. 2a). The direction and velocity of ocean currents play important roles in explaining gene flow between populations26. We defined direction deviation (ΔD) as the angle between the direction of ocean currents and the least-cost path line. The ΔD was calculated as the average of each grid cell along the least-cost path line, and the larger value represents the mismatch between directions of ocean currents and potential dispersal direction. The dispersal velocity (V ) was the average value of grid’s effective dispersal velocity, which was calculated as the projection of the ocean current velocity (V ) onto the direction of the path. The transit time between sites was estimated by dividing the least-cost distance by dispersal velocity (Fig. 2a).”
The written methods section is detailed and thorough. However, the provided code does not include all of the analyses; scripts for the DEG analysis, DAPC, selective sweep analysis, quantification of ocean current dynamics, gene ontology enrichment analysis, LFMM, and RDA were not in the zip file - additionally, the demographic analysis and ocean current drift modeling have no provided scripts, though again, the methods are detailed in the text. Inclusion of code used to conduct these analyses is necessary to ensure the reproducibility of the work and to ensure that the analysis is sound.
Response: We have submitted 11 R, Python or Shell scripts used in this study to figshare https://figshare.com/s/e164e7f678e789439b69. We also upload a file named readme.txt to introduce each script used in which analysis. For example, “1.Population_genetics.txt”, the script was used for population genetic analysis like SNP calling, filtering, TreeMix, Admixture, Dsuite, and Selective sweep analysis. “8.DEGs.R” is the R script used for DEG analysis.
Overall: Overall, the work integrates concepts across the fields of oceanography and ecological genomics to gain a more comprehensive understanding of how rafting species disperse, adapt, and respond to shifting climates, particularly ocean currents and salinity. While some of the conclusions of the work are well supported by the analyses conducted, many others are not, namely the genetic offsets, the salinity experiments and subsequent plasticity analyses, and the dispersal modeling. In addition to potential reanalysis of these data and separation of the experimental salinity work from the population genomic and dispersal/current modeling work, this manuscript would benefit from a more nuanced discussion of the caveats and limitations of the methods used and the results found, and from more explicit descriptions and definitions of relevant terminology and analyses in the main body of the text.
Response: Thank you very much for your constructive comments, which greatly improved our manuscript. We have revised the manuscript thoroughly, including reanalyzed the genomic offset section, used the coastal species to perform salinity experiments and plasticity analysis. We also added several discussions about the plasticity and local adaptation, limitation of GEA, and added more biological descriptions to some terminology, and moved the descriptions of methods and software to the Methods section. We also streamlined the Discussion section to strengthen the framework in Figure 6.
Detailed comments:
Line 81: “Based on these high-quality SNPs” is a bit unclear, do the authors mean that they used the high quality SNPs to do the analyses they mention next?
Response: We used stringent quality filter methods to filter SNPs, including keep only biallelic SNPs with the following filtering criteria: (1) minQ > 30, (2) read depth > 5, (3) max-missing counts = 5, (4) SNPs at least 5 bp away from indel regions. we also performed a linkage disequilibrium based SNP pruning to keep high quality SNPs.
Therefore, we changed our description as “Based on retained SNPs after stringent quality-filtering”.
Line 129: Given the claim of stepping stone dispersal, it would be nice to do an analysis confirming IBD
Response: We have done Mantel tests to investigate the relationship between geographical distance and gene flow, but we didn’t find significant evidence of isolation by distance (Fig. 1g, Mantel statistic r=-0.06306, P=0.53333).
However, when we used the ΔD and V that calculated from quantified ocean currents methods to plot with gene flow, we found the ΔD and V of ocean currents in June show a significant correlation with gene flow (Fig. 2c), and the mantel test also show significant relationship (ΔD: Mantel statistic r=0.6836, P=0.016667; V : Mantel statistic r=0.6617, P=0.016667). These suggest the species’ dispersal was not random but driven by the ocean currents.
Line 140: include a more definitive definition of genomic offset to better characterize what these results mean - i.e. what would a higher or lower offset mean? How does gradient forest define genomic offset?
Response: (1) We have explained the terminology in the “Results” section as follows. “To test how rafting crustaceans will respond to future oceanographic change (in the absence of plasticity), we calculated local, forward and reverse genetic offsets29. Specifically, local offset represents the mismatch between current and predicted future genomic variation in the absence of migration. By contrast, forward genetic offset represents the minimum genetic change a population would experience if migrating to a relatively favorable future location, with high values indicating strong mismatches between contemporary and future genetic compositions. Thirdly, reverse genetic offset seeks to assess whether the genotypes required to adapt to future environments already exist within contemporary populations.”
(2) In the “Materials and methods” section, we claimed how does gradient forest define genomic offset as “Based on the identified environment-associated SNPs, we used the gradient forest models to calculate the genetic offset and predict how allele frequencies would shift under future oceanographic change. We transformed the oceanographic variables from each of the four climate scenarios (2050 SSP1-2.6, 2100 SSP1-2.6, 2050 SSP5-8.5, and 2100 SSP5-8.5) into genetic importance and calculated the Euclidean distance between the present and future genomic importance values for each grid, which served as a metric of genetic offset.”
Line 146: Clarify the difference between local, forward, and reverse offset in biologically relevant terms
Response: We have added more explanation in the “Results” section in our revised manuscript as: “Specifically, local offset represents the mismatch between current and predicted future genomic variation in the absence of migration. By contrast, forward genetic offset represents the minimum genetic change a population would experience if migrating to a relatively favorable future location, with high values indicating strong mismatches between contemporary and future genetic compositions. Thirdly, reverse genetic offset seeks to assess whether the genotypes required to adapt to future environments already exist within contemporary populations.”
Line 161: Why was the cutoff for dispersal direction deviation 90º - what is the biological relevance here?
Response: We defined direction deviation (ΔD) as the angle between the direction of ocean currents and the least-cost path line. The ΔD was calculated as the average of each grid cell along the least-cost path line, which would be a score between zero and 180°, and the larger value represents the mismatch between directions of ocean currents and potential dispersal direction. As the following plot, ∆D equal to 90° means the two directions are perpendicular, while ∆D larger than 90° represents the ocean currents bearings opposite to the dispersal direction.
We have added explanations and changed the sentence as “Based on annual mean ocean current data under 2100 SSP5-8.5 scenarios, we found that 86.95% of populations will face dispersal-direction deviations (ΔD) exceeding 90°, preventing them from reaching suitable future habitats (Fig. 3d, Supplementary Fig. 14, and Supplementary Table 14).”

Response: we added some discussion about Pleistocene sea-level fluctuations and Wallace’s Line in the “Discussion” section: “During the early Pleistocene, sea-level decline exposed the Sundaland landmass, connecting coastlines of Vietnam-Thailand and Borneo19, and isolating the VT+SB+NB clade from the EB and SS populations (Supplementary Fig. 4). Subsequent sea-level rise created new intertidal zones around Borneo, enabling coastal talitrids to expand their ranges; the NB and SB lineages likely diverged from VT around 1.78 Ma. A subsequent split between NB and SB at ~0.66 Ma aligns with sea-level fluctuations during the Naynayxungla Glaciation (0.78–0.50 Ma)40, when land bridges between the Malay Peninsula and Borneo likely drove regional isolation. In addition to historical sea-level fluctuations, Wallace’s line has long been regarded as a barrier for marine and terrestrial species in the IAA42,43, even for species with extended pelagic larval dispersal44. In our study, the relatively deep genetic split between SS+EB and VT+SB+NB implies that modern oceanographic circulation in IAA has failed to fully erase these historical biogeographic patterns. Nevertheless, our analyses provide evidence of ongoing rafting-mediated gene flow between populations across the region (Fig. 1e, f).”

Line 438: The authors define groups here based on K=3, but used K=5 for all other analyses and recovered K=5 in their population structure analyses
Response: We used K=3 to simplify the prior in Fastsimcoal model simulations, because when we set K=5, there are too many models (> 100) to be simulated. According to the models which generated by K=3, we also set 25 models used K=5.
Based on the model comparisons, we found the northward dispersal from South Sulawesi to Vietnam/Thailand with South Borneo as the stepping stone is also the best models, which is similar to the K=3.
Line 501: It is unclear to me what is meant by “transforming multidimensional climatic variables into multidimensional genetic space” - I assume this is part of variable selection, but an actual description of this method would be helpful
Response: The GF (Ellis et al. 2012) methods are founded on the common idea of modelling compositional turnover using nonlinear functions of environmental gradients. These turnover functions provide a means to transform environmental variables to a common biological scale of compositional turnover (in this case, turnover in allele frequencies), thereby allowing conversion from multidimensional environmental space to multidimensional genetic space while selecting and weighting variables such that they best summarise genomic variation. By applying the associated turnover function to each mapped environmental variable, these functions can be used to map expected patterns of genomic variation, including under scenarios of future climate to assess potential impacts to locally adapted genetic variants in a spatially explicit manner.(Fitzpatrick and Keller, 2015).
Therefore, we have changed the sentence as: “Then, we used turnover function in GF models to convert complex climate data into patterns of genetic variation (allele frequencies), subsequently to select and weight these variables to best summarize genomic variation. ”
Line 501: It seems like the authors did not scale the climate variables before using them in GEA/genetic offset analysis, which would allow for a more accurate comparison of their influence on the response variables within the analysis
Response: We used Z-Score standardization methods X’= (X-μ) /δ to scale the climate variables, while X is original value, μ is mean of the original data, δ is standard deviation of the original data, and X’ is the scaled standardized value. In our revised manuscripts, we have reanalyzed the whole part of genetic offset and climate analysis based on the scaled variables and all the figures were replotted based on the new data.

Reviewer #5 (Remarks to the Author):
The study investigates how the rafting crustacean Talorchestia martensii adapts to climate change in the Indo-Australian Archipelago. The authors combined ecological modeling and genomics to explore the dispersal patterns and adaptive mechanisms of rafting species under rapid environmental changes. From 203 samples collected across the region, five geographically distinct T. martensii populations were identified. Simulations revealed stronger northward migration patterns to shape the populations compared to random or southward dispersal. Using a quantified model and particle trajectory simulations, the authors further confirmed asymmetric northward gene flow, particularly during summer monsoons, consistent with seasonal ocean currents.
Genomic data from the identified populations revealed that salinity fluctuations acted as a major selective pressure during rafting dispersal. The authors utilized transcriptome data from salinity stress experiments to identify genes associated with salinity adaptation, such as GRIK2 and SLC6A13. However, the lack of statistical significance tests and functional validation raises concerns regarding the robustness of these findings.
Response: Thank you very much for your valuable and insightful suggestions. We have made major revisions as below according to your suggestions:
(1) We have added statistical significance tests to all the analyses needed and provided the P-values or adjusted P-values. For example, in the Supplementary Fig. 20, we have added the P-values for each gene that showed differential expression with increasing treatment duration.
(2) We constructed GRIK2 dataset based on 12 genomes of amphipods, which occur in freshwater, marine and terrestrial habitats. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that these GRIK2 sequences clustered strongly by habitat type (freshwater; marine; terrestrial) rather than reflecting the underlying species phylogeny (Supplementary Fig. 18b), providing further support for this gene’s role in amphipod salinity adaptation.

ALT: Alternate allele, REF: Reference allele. b, The GRIK2 phylogeny based on 1:1 orthologs in 12 amphipod genomes suggests that species were clustered by freshwater, marine, and terrestrial habitats.
(3) In addition to the salinity stress experiments (35, 20, 10, 5 ppt) for coastal T. cf. martensii, we performed long-time salinity treatments for T. cf. martensii to 15 days and 30 days in 20 ppt to further test for salinity plasticity relevant to long-lived natural rafting voyages. The related results can be found in Fig. 4 and the following point-by-point response.
(4) We added more comparative genomics analyses between rafting and non-rafting species to gain a broader set of key genes involved in driftwood digestion, including searching the whole of CAZyme repertoire and comparing the CAZyme family composition between six rafting and three non-rafting species, gene family expansion and extraction analysis (Fig. 5b,c).

(5) We collected five tissues (antennae, brain, gut, leg, and gill) for RNA-sequencing and compared the expression of wood-feeding genes. We found that the GH genes showed a higher expression in the gut tissues. Overall, this is a well-executed study on the adaptation of rafting crustaceans, and the manuscript should be considered for publication after addressing the following comments:

Line 186: The duration of salinity stress experiments (24, 48, and 72 hours) seems too short to reflect long-term acclimation. Given that rafting voyages can last for months, a longer experimental period would better represent natural conditions.
Response: Thanks for your wonderful suggestions. We added salinity stress experiments for coastal species T. cf. martensii. The salinity gradients included 35, 20, 10, 5 ppt. We first used short-term salinity stress experiments (24, 48, and 72 hours) to show the rapid salinity shifts during rafting process. We describe the plastic expression based on these experiments as “These dynamic expression changes highlight transcriptional plasticity36 (Fig. 4g–l, Supplementary Fig. 19c–f), with the stronger shifts linked to the larger salinity shifts (Fig. 4k) and longer treatments (Fig. 4l).”
In addition to salinity stress experiments on 24, 48, 72h, we have performed salinity treatments under 15 days and 30 days in 20 ppt for coastal T. cf. Martensii in our revised manuscripts. Major results as follows:
(1) Relatively strong expression shifts were detected at low salinities (Fig. 4h) and over the longest treatments (Fig. 4i). Moreover, the number of genes enriched in ion channel transport pathways increased as treatment time increased (Fig. 4j, Supplementary Table 19).

(2) These dynamic expression changes highlight transcriptional plasticity36 (Fig. 4g–l, Supplementary Fig. 19c–f), with the stronger shifts linked to the larger salinity shifts (Fig. 4k) and longer treatments (Fig. 4l).
Specifically, the V-type H+ ATP genes related to proton transport showed decreased expression with increasing treatment duration (VATA, VATB, VATE, VATG, VATO). Notably, genes involved in the transport of small molecules (Tret1, ABCA3, HXT1) and inorganic ion (Sodium/hydrogen exchanger, Sodium/Potassium/Chloride Transporter and KCAB2) showed increased expression in these treatments (Fig. 4l, Supplementary Fig. 20, and Supplementary Table 20).

(3) Based on these results, we added Discussion as “We found increasing differential expression of genes in response to decreasing salinity, with evidence that gills function as the major osmoregulatory organs in maintaining homeostasis under fluctuating salinity58,59. Nevertheless, theoretical studies suggest that, in the longer term, plasticity may slow or constrain populations’ adaptive genetic response to environmental stress61. Therefore, we propose that both short-term (plastic) responses to temporal environmental variation, and longer-lasting adaptive responses to local conditions, should be integrated to understand how rafting species may disperse and respond to future climates.”

Response: In our revised manuscript, we reanalyzed the GEA analysis and found 459 genes showed significant correlation with the salinity. Among these genes, we found 32 genes showed differential expression between high salinity (35ppt) and low salinity (two genes in 5 ppt, 30 genes in 10 ppt). Among these 32 genes, 18 genes (56.25%) show differential expression between the high and low salinity gradients in the terrestrial species M. aosen. Among these 18 genes, 16 genes show the same upregulated or downregulated trends in both species.
Therefore, according to the expression changes related to salinity changes in two species, we thought talitrids would use a similar genetic strategy to overcome the salinity changes.

Line 215: It would be interesting to see how gene expression changes under longer treatments. This could provide insights into whether plastic responses increase over time.
Response: In addition to salinity stress experiments on 24, 48, 72h, we have performed salinity treatments under 15 days and 30 days in 20 ppt for coastal T. cf. Martensii in our revised manuscripts.
We have added Results as “To further test for salinity plasticity relevant to long-lived natural rafting voyages, we undertook extended stress experiments lasting for 15 and 30 days. Relatively strong expression shifts were detected at low salinities (Fig. 4h) and over the longest treatments (Fig. 4i). Moreover, the number of genes enriched in ion channel transport pathways increased as treatment time increased (Fig. 4j, Supplementary Table 19). Specifically, the V-type H+ ATP genes related to proton transport showed decreased expression with increasing treatment duration (VATA, VATB, VATE, VATG, VATO). Notably, genes involved in the transport of small molecules (Tret1, ABCA3, HXT1) and inorganic ion (Sodium/hydrogen exchanger, Sodium/Potassium/Chloride Transporter and KCAB2) showed increased expression in these treatments (Fig. 4l, Supplementary Fig. 20, and Supplementary Table 20).”
We also added Discussion as “We found increasing differential expression of genes in response to decreasing salinity, with evidence that gills function as the major osmoregulatory organs in maintaining homeostasis under fluctuating salinity58,59. Rapid gene expression shifts suggest plasticity may be a key prerequisite for successful rafting, at least in the short term60 (Fig. 6c). Nevertheless, theoretical studies suggest that, in the longer term, plasticity may slow or constrain populations’ adaptive genetic response to environmental stress61. Therefore, we propose that both short-term (plastic) responses to temporal environmental variation, and longer-lasting adaptive responses to local conditions, should be integrated to understand how rafting species may disperse and respond to future climates.”
Line 218: Are there significance tests for these genes? Including statistical validation would strengthen the interpretation of results.
Response: We reported these genes as differentially expressed genes, which were identified using “DESeqDataSetFromMatrix” and “DESeq” functions in the R package DESeq2. The threshold value of these DEGs was set to P-value < 0.05 and absolute of fold change ≥ 2 (log2|FC| ≥1). Log2(FC) ≥ 1 indicates upregulation, and log2(FC) ≤ -1 indicates downregulation. In the revised manuscript, we used new genes to show gradient changes along the duration gradients and added P-value on the graph.
Supplementary Fig. 20. Expression changes of salinity-related genes. Gradually up-regulated expression genes (red) involved in small molecular exchange along increased duration. Gradually down-regulated expression of V-type H+-ATPases encoding genes (blue) along with increased duration treatments. Gene expression level was scaled use log (FPKM+1). The P-value means significant expression 2 changes between the short term treatments (24 hours) and long term treatments (30 days).
Lines 332-333: This section seems a bit weak to me. The discussion on wood degradation genes seems narrowly focused on a few candidates. Whole-genome comparisons between rafting and non-rafting species would help identify a broader set of key genes involved in driftwood digestion.
Response: (1) To gain a comparison of a broader set of key genes involved in driftwood digestion, we searched the six rafting species (T. martensii, Trinorchestia longiramus, Florersorchestia mkomani, Cochinorchestia sp., Platorchestia pacifica, and Morinoia aosen) and three non-rafting species genomes (Hyalella azteca, Parhyale hawaiensis, and Hirondellea gigas) for Carbohydrate Active Enzymes (CAZymes) belonging to glycosyl hydrolases (GHs), carbohydrate esterases, auxiliary activities, along with associated carbohydrate-binding modules and glycosyl transferases. The CAZyme family composition was largely conserved between rafting and non-rafting species; however, the copy number of CAZyme genes varied notably (Supplementary Fig. 21).
Supplementary Fig. 21. The proportion and detailed number of CAZymes between rafting and non-rafting species.
(2) We also compared the number of CAZyme repertoire between rafting and non-rafting species. We found there are 16 GHs, three carbohydrate esterases, and two auxiliary activities exist in all six rafting and three non-rafting species. In particular, rafting species exhibited significantly higher proportions of GH genes compared to non-rafting species (Fig. 5c, Supplementary Table 21).
Fig. 5 Horizontal gene transfer and gene duplication of GH gene families. b, The reconstructed species tree based on three non-rafting and six rafting talitrid genomes. c, Comparisons of abundances of GH gene families in all cazymes suggest rafting talitrids have more GHs than the non-rafting species (Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
(4) Based on the genome sequence of these rafting and non-rafting species, we also performed gene family expansion analysis, and we found the 89 gene families that were significantly expanded in the rafting species (P<0.05), and GH7 gene family is one of them. Therefore, we thought it is reasonable to propose that GH7 is one of the key genes in the wood feeding of rafting species. We also found a lot of genes participate in the carbon metabolism (22 genes) and the citric acid (TCA) cycle (six genes), which suggest more key genes would be involved in the energy generation and usage.

The discussion is fairly weak, I would expect to see more discussion on how biotic interactions (e.g., competition) affect rafting success; comparisons between salinity adaptation mechanisms in T. martensii and other marine species; the evolutionary history of GRIK2 and its role in other species.
Response: We have reconstructed and streamlined the whole discussion. According to your suggestions, major changes are as follows:
(1) As far as how biotic interactions (e.g., competition) affect rafting success, we have added Discussion as: “In addition to physiological plasticity, competition for space and food on the driftwood also influences rafting success62. The slender morphology of T. martensii (< 15mm) likely facilitates their crypsis on and in driftwood, minimizing potential predation by birds or fish63. Furthermore, their fecundity (10-20 eggs per female) and rapid generation time likely enhance the survival of rafting populations. Crucially, the ability of this species to feed on driftwood, enables lengthy rafting voyages64. In particular, the high proportion of key GH genes that are highly expressed in the gut emphasizes the key role of wood feeding in this rafting system (Fig. 6c).”
(2) As far as comparisons between salinity adaptation mechanisms in T. martensii and other marine species, we first compared the salinity adaptation gene changes of T. martensii with M. aosen, “The original habitat of T. martensii is marine and high salinity environments (ca. 35 ppt). Compared with the control samples, we found more genes would show differential expression as the salinity decreased to 20, 10 and 5 ppt, it means an increase of environment stress induces broader transcriptional responses (Fig. 4g, h). A similar pattern was found in the Morinoia aosen, a terrestrial species, with more gene expression changes in response to salinity shifts from low to high salinity stress (Supplementary Fig. 19). The salinity experiments from two species provide robust evidence that talitrids would use some plastic osmoregulatory mechanism to cope with the salinity stress.”
Then, we added Discussion of gills as the osmoregulatory organ similar to other crustaceans. “Thus, we propose that amphipod gills may be crucial osmoregulatory organs, with comparable differential expression pattern between tissues also detected in the terrestrial talitrid, M. aosen (Supplementary Fig. 19b).”
We also referenced other marine organisms (Atlantic killifish, Fundulus heteroclitus) that use plastic strategies to adapt to salinity changes. “Rapid gene expression shifts suggest plasticity may be a key prerequisite for successful rafting, at least in the short term60 (Fig. 6c). Nevertheless, theoretical studies suggest that, in the longer term, plasticity may slow or constrain populations’ adaptive genetic response to environmental stress61.”
(3) As far as the evolutionary history of GRIK2 and its role in other species, we used blastp method to search the 1:1 orthologs in another 11 amphipod genomes, which belong to freshwater, marine, and terrestrial habitats and could be a perfect model for us to compare the gene's role in salinity adaptation. We aligned the protein and reconstructed the phylogenetic relationship between these species.
We have added the phylogeny to the supplementary figures and added results description. “We used BLASTp to detect 1:1 orthologs in the genomes of 11 additional amphipod taxa, encompassing a variety of freshwater, marine and terrestrial habitats. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that these GRIK2 sequences clustered strongly by habitat type (freshwater; marine; terrestrial) rather than reflecting the underlying species phylogeny (Supplementary Fig. 18b), providing further support for this gene’s role in amphipod salinity adaptation.”
Lines 348-349: Could the authors quantify the expression dosage of duplicated genes in T. martensii and compare it to species with fewer gene copies?
Response: To quantify the expression levels of duplicated genes, we sequenced the transcriptomes of five tissues (gut, gills, legs, brains, and antennae) from three species, Parhyale hawaiensis, Talorchestia martensii, and Morinoia aosen. We compared the GH7 expression between different tissues, and found the GH7 genes show higher expression in their gut system than the gills, legs, brains, and antennae. Besides, we detected similar expression levels between different copies for non-rafting and rafting species in the same duplication events in the same duplication events (Fig. 5f, Supplementary Fig. 22). Considering the larger number of GH7 copies and their expression in the gut, we proposed these duplication events increased gene dosage.
We have added Results description as “Moreover, transcriptome analysis revealed that GH7, GH9, and GH30_1 gene copies are highly expressed in the gut, with comparable expression levels in rafting species despite their greater gene copy numbers relative to non-rafting species (Fig. 5f, Supplementary Fig. 22).”

REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The study "Genomics of rafting crustaceans in tropical oceans: adapting to marine climate change" uses an interdisciplinary approach combining ecogenomics, population genetics, dispersal and oceanography simulations and modeling, and salinity stress experiments. The authors have satisfactorily addressed all comments.
My only concern is that the LD threshold used appears too low, and I would expect a justification for this choice in the Methods section. Statistically, an r² ≥ 0.5 is considered sufficient to avoid LD, as values above 0.5 occur in less than 14% of the allelic frequency space (VanLieren & Rosenberg 2008. Theor. Popul. Biol. 74:130). Using a lower threshold can only be justified in specific cases, such as very large sampled populations. A brief explanation of this choice should be added to the text. That aside, I consider the manuscript acceptable for publication.
Response: Thank you for your wonderful suggestions. In the Plink software, --ld-window-r2 controls the r2 threshold for a variant-pair to be included in the report. The default setting is 0.2. Although this value might be considered relatively low, when we used a window-sliding based method in 50bp, using an r² threshold of 0.2 helps to reduce the impact of physical linkage while preserving enough independent markers for the following population structure inference. We also employed an r² threshold of 0.5 for population structure analysis, and found that the inferred structure (K=5) was nearly identical to that derived from the two comparison values.
We have changed the sentence in the Materials and methods section as “We further excluded highly correlated SNPs by performing linkage disequilibrium based SNP pruning in PLINK v.1.9.078 with a default pairwise r2 threshold 0.2. This threshold reduces LD-induced bias while preserving enough independent genetic markers to accurately infer population structure, an approach previously used in marine genomic studies79.”
Figure. Admixture analysis based on the SNPs after linkage disequilibrium pruning using threshold 0.2 (a) and 0.5 (b).

The code seems fine. There is a README file with brief explanations of each file.
Response: Thank you very much.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
I am very pleased with the revisions. Thank you, and congratulations on all your hard work.
Response: Thank you for your wonderful comments.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The revised manuscript addresses many of the concerns raised in the previous review, and is a robust and comprehensive exploration of the genomics of rafting crustaceans. Overall, the integration of interdisciplinary data in this manuscript is a clear strength. Putting all this data together was clearly a lot of work, and the authors are to be commended for the synthesis. With some further clarification of the limitations of the offset analysis, particularly emphasizing how their interpretation is debated, this will make a nice contribution to the literature.
Response: Thank you for your wonderful suggestions. We have made corrections according to your suggestions.
Comments:
Framework: The new figure (Fig. 6) describing the study’s framework better synthesizes the study’s design, making it more easily reproduced in future studies on rafting species. Additionally, the revised sentence in the abstract better reflects what is presented in the manuscript. This resolves the previous comment that the study does not put forward a framework in the text.
Response: Thank you for your wonderful suggestions.
GEA analysis: The updated GEA results are robust and comprehensive, and the added discussion better reflects the limitations of these analyses in rafting species. The GEA results presented here are consistent with the results from other analyses in this study and justified given the recovery of population structure. The authors could draw a parallel between rafting species and other high-dispersal marine species (e.g. Strongylocentrotus purpuratus, Chlorostoma funebralis, & Semibalanus balanoides), which have been shown to exhibit local adaptation despite high dispersal/gene flow.
Response: We have added a parallel between rafting species and other high-dispersal marine species in the Discussion section “These results also revealed signatures of local adaptation in rafting species despite their high dispersal potential, which align with previous studies of other high-dispersal marine species, such as Strongylocentrotus purpuratus56, Chlorostoma funebralis57, and Semibalanus balanoides58.”
Genomic Offset analysis: The revised text on the different types of genomic offsets is helpful and appropriately clarifies the difference between forward, reverse, and local genetic offsets. The addition to the methods on how ocean current and genomic offset analyses are linked is helpful in clarifying how the two were integrated, however the manuscript would benefit from including a brief summary of the information that is only provided in the response to reviewers.
Response: We have added a brief summary as “Based on the GF results, we integrated forward genetic offset with ocean current modelling to calculate directional deviation (ΔD) between ocean currents and least-cost dispersal paths, to assess rafting potential of T. martensi to suitable habitats. In the absence of land barriers, the least-cost path was calculated as the Euclidean distance between two sites. By contrast, when this path was interrupted by land barriers, the least-cost path was inferred from oceanographic connectivity.”
The new discussion points provide important caveats about these results and I appreciate the call to further validate these methods in marine systems, although a number of claims by the authors need revision before this can be published. First, offsets do not measure or predict “long-term evolutionary responses to broader environmental variation”, nor do they measure “genetic variations required for long-term adaptation of future climate change”. Rather, they are a measure of an environmental distance, weighted by environments that correlate most strongly with genetic structure, and the interpretation is debated (see papers by Matt Fitzpatrick, papers by Lotterhos, especially Lotterhos 2024 Interpretation issues with “genomic vulnerability” arise from conceptual issues in local adaptation and maladaptation, see Rellstab et al 2021: Prospects and limitations of genomic offset in conservation management, see Hoffman et al: Opportunities and challenges in assessing climate change vulnerability through genomics). In addition, whether the finding of strong outlier loci justifies the use of genomic offsets is debatable: whether offsets correlate with fitness changes in new environments depends on patterns of local adaptation in the metapopulation, the fitness landscape, and other biological responses such as plasticity. In addition, despite many other studies predicting genomic offset to future climates, it is important to note that these analyses do not account for adaptive evolution, instead assuming an instantaneous environmental change. Thus, genomic offsets are not necessarily a reflection of long-term genetic adaptation. The manuscript would benefit from some further acknowledgement of these limitations in using genomic offsets to predict responses to future climates.
Response: Thank you very much for your constructive comments. We now note more clearly that genetic offsets are a measure of environmental distance weighted by environments that correlate most strongly with genetic structure. It shows the instantaneous degree of maladaptation of a genome when moved from the environment to which it is adapted into a new environment.
